What? You've been going on like this and you don't even have any proof?
You still don't know how to use your head, do you.
Why don't you think about it a little harder.
That's it! You and he are the same height!
Your height is the same. Almost nobody is as short as you are!
Yeah... you have the same voice. That's it.
Your voice sounds just like his.

Well, that's really too bad!
I know... the two of you talk the same way.
Your accent and word choice is just like his!
Yeah... that wormy, untrustworthy attitude of yours is just like him.

I've got it! You smell just like him!
Huh? Gillian, what did Napoleon smell like?

I'd know that B.O. anywhere... You're Napoleon!

Beryllium, nitrogen, sulfur, oxygen... I've got it!
Gillian, let's go over the names of these elements, shall we?
I'll tell you again, these are Chinese characters for elements.
The character on the left is Beryllium. The next one, and the last one are Nitrogen. The third one is Sulfur. The fourth one is Oxygen.
In the order they're written: Beryllium, Nitrogen, Sulfur, Oxygen, Nitrogen.
It's a simple code using Chinese characters for chemical elements.
Jeez... that's pathetic. oh well, I guess I gotta help you.
That spells 'BENSON'.
In other words, when you line up the symbols, you get 'BENSON'...
The point isn't their names, but their chemical symbols. Nitrogen is N. Beryllium is Be. Oxygen is O. Sulfur is S. Get it?
In their original order, Be for beryllium, N for nitrogen, S for sulfur, O for oxygen and N for nitrogen.
So if you line them up in this order... Beryllium's 'Be', Nitrogen's 'N', Sulfur's 'S', Oxygen's 'O', Nitrogen's 'N'.
...get it yet?
C'mon, you should at least know that the symbols for the elements are usually written using letters, right?.
